إخلاء المسؤولية القانونية

تمت كتابة هذا الكتاب للتفكير العاطفي والوعي الشخصي وفهم العلاقات. إنه ليس بديلاً عن الاستشارة المهنية أو علاج الأزواج أو العلاج النفسي أو المشورة القانونية أو الرعاية الطبية. القصص والأسماء والشخصيات في كل فصل خيالية بالكامل وتم إنشاؤها للتوضيح التعليمي والعاطفي فقط. أي تشابه مع أشخاص حقيقيين، أحياء أو أموات، هو من قبيل الصدفة البحتة.

يخلي المؤلف والناشر والموزع صراحة مسؤوليتهم عن أي ضرر ينشأ عن استخدام أو تطبيق الأفكار الواردة في هذا الكتاب. كل علاقة فريدة من نوعها. ما يتردد صداه بالنسبة لشخص ما قد لا ينطبق على شخص آخر. هذا الكتاب ليس دليلاً لاتخاذ قرارات حياتية مهمة. إنها دعوة للتأمل بصدق ولطف في تجربتك الداخلية.

إذا كنت أنت أو أي شخص تعرفه تعاني من العنف المنزلي، أو العنف العاطفي، أو الاكتئاب الشديد، أو إيذاء النفس، أو أي موقف يتعلق بالسلامة الشخصية، فيرجى طلب المساعدة المهنية المؤهلة على الفور. هذا الكتاب ليس مصدرا للأزمات.

المقدمة: لكل امرأة تجد طريقها

عزيزي،

لا أحد يخبرك بالحقيقة الكاملة عن الحياة بعد الزفاف. يتحدثون عن الفستان والطعام والزهور والصور. إنهم لا يتحدثون عن الصباح التالي، عندما تهدأ الضوضاء وينظر شخصان إلى بعضهما البعض عبر حياة مشتركة ويفكران بهدوء: ماذا الآن؟

لقد كتب هذا الكتاب لتلك اللحظة. ولكل اللحظات التي تليها. الحجج الصغيرة التي تبدو وكأنها تتعلق بالأطباق ولكنها في الحقيقة تتعلق بالشعور بأنك غير مرئي. الصمت على مائدة العشاء ليس سلميًا ولكنه بعيد. الحب الموجود بصدق ولكنه ليس كافيًا إلى حد ما لوقف الوحدة. النسخة التي تخشى أن تفقدها من نفسك، والنسخة التي تصبح عليها ببطء وعصبية.

يتبع كل فصل في هذا الكتاب نوعًا حقيقيًا من النساء خلال لحظة حقيقية. اسمها مختلف في كل مرة. حالتها محددة. لكن شيئًا ما بداخلها سوف يبدو مألوفًا لك، لأن ما تشعر به، تشعر به العديد من النساء ويتحملنه بهدوء دون العثور على كلمات تعبر عنه. يقدم هذا الكتاب تلك الكلمات.

Read it slowly. With honesty. With kindness for yourself. You are not failing at marriage. You are learning it. And learning, no matter how uncomfortable, is always a form of love.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

How to Use This Book

This is not a self-help manual with checklists and action plans. It is a book of stories, and the best way to use it is the way you would read a letter from a trusted friend who happens to understand both psychology and the quiet weight of daily married life.

You may read from beginning to end, following the arc from early marriage through conflict, boundaries, loneliness, and renewal. Or you may open it at the chapter whose title feels most like your own life today. Both approaches are right. Go where your heart needs to go.

After each story, sit with what you felt. Notice which line made you catch your breath. Notice which character reminded you of yourself, or your partner, or someone you wish one of you could be. That noticing is where understanding begins. And understanding, gently pursued, is where things start to change.

Part I: The Wedding Ends, Real Life Begins

Chapter 1: When Marriage Felt Different Than Expected

My dear,

Aarohi thought she knew what marriage would feel like.

She had imagined warmth. Togetherness. A soft landing after long days.

Marriage was not bad. But it was different.

After the wedding, life moved fast. Work resumed. Responsibilities appeared. Relatives faded away.

Romance did not disappear. It changed shape.

Aarohi noticed it in small ways. Less time to talk. More decisions to make. More adjustments than she expected.

Her husband, Nikhil, was kind. Supportive. Practical.

Yet sometimes, she felt unsettled. Not unhappy. Just unsure.

Psychologically, early marriage brings identity shock. Two lives merge. Old rhythms break. New ones feel unfamiliar.

Aarohi did not talk about this much. She felt guilty. Everyone said marriage was a blessing.

"What is wrong with me?" she wondered.

Some nights, she lay awake beside Nikhil. He slept peacefully. Her mind stayed active.

She missed her old independence. Her spontaneity. Her quiet space.

This scared her. She loved Nikhil. Why did she miss herself?

One evening, while cooking together, she said casually, "Do you feel different after marriage?"

Nikhil paused. "Yes," he said honestly. "I feel more responsible. Less carefree."

That surprised her.

They talked more that night. Not deeply. But openly.

Aarohi shared how she felt stretched. Pulled between who she was and who she was becoming.

Nikhil admitted he felt pressure to be stable. Strong. Always certain.

Both were adjusting silently.

That night changed something small but important. Aarohi realized she was not failing at marriage. She was learning it.

Marriage was not a feeling. It was a transition.

She also learned this. Missing your old self does not mean you regret your partner.

It means your identity is reshaping.

Over the next weeks, they made space for individuality. Separate hobbies. Time alone. No guilt.

Aarohi felt lighter. Not because marriage became perfect. But because she stopped judging herself.

Early marriage is confusing for many women. Love exists. But so does grief for the old self.

Both can coexist.

Aarohi understood something gently. Marriage does not erase you. It asks you to renegotiate who you are.

And when that negotiation is done with honesty and kindness, marriage stops feeling like loss and starts feeling like expansion.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 2: When Work Followed Her Home

My dear,

Ritika loved her work. It gave her confidence. Independence. A sense of identity.

Marriage did not change that. But it changed how tired she felt.

By the time she reached home, her mind was still at the office. Deadlines. Messages. Meetings replaying inside her head.

Her husband, Karan, noticed it first in silence. Dinner conversations became shorter. Replies slower. Her eyes often looked distant.

Ritika did not mean to disconnect. She was just carrying too much.

Psychologically, when women in their 20s and 30s work full-time, they often live in constant mental switching. Professional self. Partner self. Family self.

Switching costs energy.

One evening, Karan said lightly, "You 're here, but you 're not really here."

Ritika felt defensive rise instantly. "I 'm doing my best," she replied.

Both were right. And both felt misunderstood.

That night, Ritika lay awake. Her body was tired. Her mind restless.

She felt guilty. Guilty for wanting career growth. Guilty for not being fully present. Guilty for feeling resentful of guilt itself.

Many women know this emotional loop.

The next day, Ritika spoke differently. Not from irritation. From honesty.

"I feel like I 'm failing everywhere," she said quietly. "At work, I 'm pressured. At home, I 'm distracted."

Karan softened immediately. "I don 't need you perfect," he said. "I just want to feel connected."

That sentence mattered.

They talked about boundaries. Not rules. But protection.

No office calls during dinner. A short pause after coming home before switching roles. Ten minutes of quiet together before phones came out.

Small changes. But intentional.

Ritika noticed something shift. When she stopped carrying work into the bedroom, her body relaxed. Her tone softened.

Karan noticed too. She smiled more. Touched more. Listened with ease.

Ritika also learned something important. Loving her work did not mean loving stress. And protecting her relationship did not mean sacrificing ambition.

Marriage did not need her exhaustion. It needed her presence.

She also stopped apologizing for being driven. Instead, she explained her inner load.

Psychologically, clarity reduces conflict. Unspoken strain creates distance.

Over time, Ritika felt more balanced. Not because life slowed down. But because she stopped living everywhere at once.

She realized something powerful. Work will always demand more. Relationships need conscious limits to survive.

And when a woman learns to arrive home emotionally, not just physically, love stops feeling like another task and starts feeling like rest.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 3: When the Screen Became the Third Person

My dear,

Ira did not hate the phone. She used it too.

Work emails. Messages. Social media. Quick escapes during tired moments.

But slowly, she noticed something unsettling.

Her husband, Aditya, sat beside her every night. Yet his attention lived elsewhere. Scrolling. Replying. Watching something without sound.

They were together. But not with each other.

At first, Ira ignored the feeling. "It 's normal," she told herself. "Everyone lives like this."

Still, her body reacted. A small ache in the chest. A quiet sadness she couldn 't explain.

She noticed it most at night. When they lay side by side. Lights off. Screens glowing.

She missed talking without interruption. Eye contact. That soft feeling of being chosen.

Psychologically, the brain reads attention as safety. When attention is divided, connection weakens quietly.

One evening, Ira spoke about her day. Aditya nodded. His eyes stayed on the screen.

She stopped mid-sentence.

That pause hurt more than words.

Later, Aditya asked, "Why did you go quiet?"

"I didn 't want to compete," she replied softly. "Not with a phone."

Aditya laughed nervously. "You 're overthinking," he said.

But Ira wasn 't angry. She was tired of feeling secondary.

That night, she spoke again. Slowly. Carefully.

"When your phone is always there," she said, "I feel like I 'm interrupting your real life."

This time, Aditya listened.

He had not realized the impact. For him, the phone was escape. From pressure. From responsibility. From thinking.

He didn 't see it as withdrawal. But it was.

They decided to try something small. Not rules. Not control.

Phones away during meals. No screens for the first fifteen minutes in bed. No scrolling while the other is speaking.

The first few days felt awkward. Silence felt loud. They did not know what to say.

That itself was revealing.

Slowly, conversation returned. Not deep talks. Small ones. Jokes. Memories. Plans.

Ira felt something soften inside her. Not excitement. Relief.

Aditya noticed something too. Being present felt grounding. Not restrictive.

Ira also learned something important. Asking for presence is not insecurity. It is a request for connection.

Aditya learned too. Attention is a form of intimacy. Not dramatic. But essential.

Phones did not disappear from their lives. Work did not reduce. Social media stayed.

But the space between them changed.

Ira realized something gentle. Love fades not from lack of feeling, but from lack of attention.

And when couples choose presence, even for small moments, connection returns.

Quietly. Naturally.

Not through effort. But through awareness.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 4: When Everything Was Fine, But She Wasn\'t

My dear,

Tara often told herself she should be grateful.

Her marriage was peaceful. No shouting. No major conflict. No fear.

Her husband, Mohit, was steady. Predictable. Kind in practical ways.

Life felt settled. Too settled.

Tara noticed the feeling during quiet moments. Sunday afternoons. Late evenings. Times when nothing demanded her attention.

She felt\... blank.

Not unhappy. Not sad. Just unmoved.

Psychologically, emotional flatness often appears when excitement fades but emotional nourishment is missing.

Tara did not miss drama. She missed engagement.

She noticed it in her body. Less enthusiasm. Less curiosity. Touch that felt automatic.

She questioned herself. "Is this how marriage is supposed to feel?" "Am I expecting too much?"

Many women in their 20s and early 30s ask these questions silently. Because nothing looks wrong from the outside.

One evening, Tara sat scrolling on her phone. Mohit sat beside her watching something. They were close. But not connected.

Suddenly, Tara felt tears rise. Unexpected. Quiet.

Mohit noticed. "What happened?" he asked.

"I don 't know," she said honestly. "I just feel\... numb."

Mohit felt alarmed. He assumed numb meant unhappy. Unhappy meant failure.

"I 'm doing everything right," he said gently.

Tara nodded. "I know. That 's why this is hard to explain."

She paused. "I don 't feel unhappy with you. I just don 't feel emotionally alive lately."

That sentence changed the conversation.

Mohit listened more carefully. He realized he had equated peace with connection. If there were no problems, he assumed love was strong.

Tara explained slowly. She missed shared excitement. New experiences. Curiosity about each other 's inner worlds.

Mohit admitted he had stopped initiating. Not because he didn 't care. But because things felt "set."

Security had turned into autopilot.

They decided to try something different. Not dramatic changes.

A weekly activity together. Trying something new each month. Talking about dreams again. Even small ones.

Slowly, Tara felt something stir. Interest. Warmth. Movement.

Not fireworks. But color returning.

Mohit noticed it too. Tara laughed more. Touched more naturally. Engaged more deeply.

Tara learned something important. Feeling flat does not mean love is gone. It often means love is under-stimulated.

Mohit learned too. Stability needs curiosity to stay alive.

Marriage does not fail only from conflict. It can also weaken from emotional stillness.

When couples notice emptiness early and respond without blame, connection deepens.

Tara realized something gentle. Love is not just about safety. It is also about shared aliveness.

And when both partners choose to move emotionally again, marriage stops feeling like a routine and starts feeling like a living bond.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi
Part II: Conflict, Stress, and the Need for Safety

Chapter 5: How the Fight Actually Started

My dear,

Riya never planned to fight that evening. She was already tired.

Work had been heavy. Traffic worse. Her mind felt crowded.

When she entered the house, she saw shoes scattered near the door. The sink was full. The light in the bedroom was still on.

Small things. Normal things.

Yet something inside her tightened.

Her husband, Armaan, sat on the sofa. Relaxed. Scrolling. He looked comfortable.

"Did you have dinner?" he asked casually.

That question landed badly.

Riya felt irritation rise instantly. Not because of the question. But because she felt unseen.

Psychologically, fights rarely start with the real issue. They start when emotional needs are unmet. Fatigue lowers patience. Stress sharpens reactions.

Riya snapped. "Can 't you see the mess?" she said.

Armaan looked surprised. "What 's wrong?" he asked.

That question made it worse.

"What 's wrong" sounded like dismissal. Like confusion instead of awareness.

Riya 's voice rose. "Why do I have to notice everything?"

Armaan felt attacked. He defended himself. "I didn 't know it mattered so much."

Now both were activated.

Riya 's anger came from overload. From carrying invisible responsibility. From feeling like the default adult.

Armaan 's defensiveness came from feeling criticized. From feeling like nothing he did was enough.

Neither said this.

Words came out sharper. Past examples entered the room. The fight grew legs.

Then something shifted.

Riya suddenly felt her chest tighten. Her throat felt heavy. She realized she was no longer angry. She was overwhelmed.

She stopped mid-sentence. "I 'm not fighting about the mess," she said quietly. "I 'm exhausted."

That pause mattered.

Armaan noticed her tone change. He softened.

"I didn 't know you were feeling this stretched," he said.

That sentence calmed half the storm.

They sat in silence for a moment. Not cold. Just honest.

Riya explained how she felt mentally responsible for everything. Planning. Remembering. Managing.

Armaan listened. Not to fix. To understand.

He realized something important. Riya was not angry at him. She was drowning in load.

They made one small change. Not a big rule. Just awareness.

Armaan would notice more. Initiate more. Not wait to be told.

Riya would speak earlier. Before resentment built.

Riya learned something valuable. Anger often hides exhaustion. When spoken early, it does not explode.

Armaan learned too. Defensiveness blocks connection. Curiosity opens it.

Fights do not mean something is wrong with love. They often mean something is wrong with balance.

When couples learn to look beneath the argument, conflict becomes information. Not destruction.

And when a woman learns to name her tiredness before it becomes anger, fights stop being battles and start becoming conversations.
With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 6: How They Learned Not to Hurt Each Other

My dear,

Aisha hated fights. Not the disagreement. The aftermath.

The silence. The tight chest. The replaying of words in her head.

Her husband, Sameer, fought differently. He raised his voice. Then shut down. He needed space.

Aisha needed reassurance. Immediately.

This mismatch made fights worse.

Psychologically, conflict styles are shaped early. Some people fight to feel heard. Some withdraw to feel safe.

But couples rarely know this.

Their arguments followed a pattern. Aisha pushed for discussion. Sameer pulled away. She felt abandoned. He felt attacked.

One evening, the fight escalated fast. A comment. A tone. A sharp reply.

Aisha felt her body heat up. Her heart raced. Her words came fast.

Sameer felt overwhelmed. His mind went blank. He said something careless.

That sentence hurt.

The room changed.

Later that night, both felt regret. Not because of the issue. But because of how they spoke.

The next day, Aisha said something different. "I don 't want us to win fights," she said. "I want us to feel safe after them."

That sentence mattered.

They talked calmly. Not about the topic. About how they fight.

Aisha explained what happens inside her body. Silence feels like rejection. Distance feels like loss.

Sameer explained his side. Raised voices make him shut down. He needs time to think.

Neither was wrong. They were wired differently.

They agreed on simple rules. Not rigid. Protective.

No name-calling. No bringing up the past. No fighting when exhausted. A pause when voices rise.

Most importantly, Sameer would say, "I need a break, but I 'm not leaving."

And Aisha would respect the pause without chasing the conversation.

This changed everything.

Fights still happened. But they softened faster.

Aisha felt safer. Even during disagreement.

Sameer felt less trapped. More willing to return and talk.

Aisha learned something important. Fighting well is not about control. It is about protection.

Sameer learned too. Pausing is useful only when followed by repair.

Marriage does not require agreement. It requires emotional safety.

When couples learn how not to fight, words stop becoming weapons. And conflict stops creating fear.

Aisha realized something gentle. You don 't need perfect communication. You need respectful intention.

And when both partners protect the relationship even during disagreement, fights lose their power to damage love.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 7: When Intimacy Needed Safety, Not Pressure

My dear,

Nandini noticed the change quietly. Not in one moment. But over weeks.

Intimacy between her and Rohan felt different. Not absent. Just tense.

She still cared. She still loved him. But her body did not respond the same way.

She felt tight instead of open. Distracted instead of present. Sometimes she avoided closeness without fully knowing why.

Rohan noticed too. He grew unsure. Then impatient.

"Are you upset with me?" he asked one night.

Nandini shook her head. "No," she said. But that was not the full truth.

Psychologically, intimacy needs emotional safety. When a woman feels pressured, her nervous system closes. Desire does not grow in anxiety.

Nandini felt guilty. She wondered if something was wrong with her. Many women do.

But deep inside, she knew. She did not feel emotionally held lately.

Life had been busy. Work stress. Family expectations. Constant mental load.

When Rohan reached for closeness, her mind was still racing. Her body could not follow.

One evening, she spoke carefully. "I need to say something honestly," she said. "Not to hurt you."

Rohan tensed. Fear showed first.

"I don 't feel distant from you," she continued. "I feel rushed inside myself."

That sentence slowed the room.

She explained gently. How stress stayed in her body. How she needed softness before closeness. Conversation. Presence. Time.

Rohan listened. Not defensively. Curiously.

He realized something important. He had been taking closeness personally. As approval or rejection. Not as a shared experience.

They decided to slow things down. No expectations. No silent pressure.

Some evenings they just talked. Some evenings they sat quietly. Some evenings they held hands without needing more.

This changed everything.

Nandini felt her body soften again. Breathing deepened. Shoulders relaxed.

Rohan noticed warmth return. Not forced. Natural.

Psychologically, when safety increases, desire follows on its own.

Nandini also learned something important. Intimacy is not a duty. It is a response.

And asking for safety is not rejection. It is honesty.

Rohan learned too. Presence is more powerful than insistence. Patience builds closeness.

Their relationship did not become perfect. But it became kinder.

Nandini realized something gentle. When intimacy is protected, not demanded, it becomes a place of rest instead of pressure.

And when a woman feels emotionally safe, her openness returns not because she tries, but because she trusts.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 8: When One Partner Was Not Okay

They talked every day. But rarely connected. Conversations stayed practical. Who will pick up whom. What needs to be paid. What is pending.

Emotionally, marriage had shifted into maintenance mode. Not intimacy mode.

Psychologically, long relationships need conscious care. Not because love fades. But because attention gets divided.

Madhuri felt tired in a different way now. Not exhausted. Under-nourished emotionally.

She missed being noticed. Not praised. Just seen.

One evening, she dressed nicely. Not for an event. Just for herself.

Anil noticed but said nothing. Not because he didn 't care. Because noticing had stopped being intentional.

That night, Madhuri felt a familiar ache. Small. Sharp.

Later, while clearing the table, she said softly, "Do you remember how we used to talk?"

Anil looked up. "We still talk," he said.

She nodded. "Yes. But we don 't meet anymore."

That sentence stayed with him.

Anil reflected deeply. He realized he showed love through responsibility. Providing. Protecting.

But he had stopped expressing warmth.

They talked slowly that night. No blame. No demand.

Madhuri spoke about emotional dryness. About feeling like a manager of life, not a partner in intimacy.

Anil listened. Not defensively. With curiosity.

He realized something important. Marriage does not maintain itself. It needs emotional servicing. Like anything valuable.

They decided on something simple. Once a week, no talk about logistics. Only about feelings. Dreams. Memories.

At first, it felt awkward. Rusty. But slowly, warmth returned.

Madhuri noticed Anil reaching out more. A message during the day. A compliment. A pause to listen.

Anil noticed Madhuri softening. Less irritation. More laughter.

Neither changed dramatically. They changed intentionally.

Long marriages don 't break suddenly. They dry quietly.

Emotional neglect is rarely intentional. It is usually accidental.

Madhuri learned something gentle. Asking for emotional care is not demanding. It is maintenance.

Anil learned too. Love expressed once is not enough for decades.

Marriage grows old beautifully when couples water it regularly. Not heavily. But consistently.

And when emotional care becomes routine, long marriages stop feeling heavy and start feeling warm again.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 21: When Routine Hid the Distance

My dear,

Sunita and Prakash had not drifted apart suddenly. They drifted slowly. So slowly that neither noticed at first.

Life was full. Children growing. Parents aging. Work demands increasing.

Days followed a pattern. Mornings rushed. Evenings tired. Nights quiet.

They shared space. Not attention.

Sunita noticed it one afternoon. While sitting alone with tea. She realized she could not remember the last time they laughed together.

Not argued. Not discussed logistics. Laughed.

Psychologically, routine creates safety. But it can also numb connection when emotional check-ins disappear.

Sunita did not blame Prakash. She knew he was tired too. But her heart felt untouched.

That evening, she asked casually, "Do you remember our first trip together?"

Prakash smiled faintly. "Yes," he said. "It rained the whole time."

They both smiled. Something softened.

That small moment mattered.

Over the next days, Sunita tried something different. Not complaints. Not reminders of distance.

She shared memories. Stories. Small jokes.

Prakash noticed. At first, he felt confused. Then curious.

One night, while washing dishes together, he said, "We don 't do things together anymore, do we?"

Sunita looked at him. "We got busy surviving," she replied.

That sentence carried truth.

They talked that night. Slowly. Without urgency.

Sunita spoke about emotional hunger. Not loneliness. But absence of shared moments.

Prakash admitted he had assumed closeness was permanent. Once built, it would always stay.

They realized something important. Connection is not a one-time achievement. It needs renewal.

They decided to start small. Not date nights. Not big plans.

Morning tea together. Evening walks once a week. Sharing one story from the day.

At first, it felt forced. Artificial. Like trying to restart an old engine.

But gradually, rhythm returned.

Sunita felt warmth again. Not excitement. Familiar closeness.

Prakash felt relief. Connection no longer felt like pressure. Just presence.

They also learned to protect these moments. No phones. No multitasking. Just being there.

Reconnection does not require romance. It requires attention.

Sunita realized something gentle. Distance does not always mean loss of love. Sometimes it means love unattended.

Prakash learned too. Routine can coexist with connection if couples choose it intentionally.

Years of routine do not end marriages. Silence does.

When couples pause, remember, and gently turn toward each other again, connection returns.

Not loudly. Not dramatically.

Quietly. Steadily.

And in that quiet reconnection, marriage finds its way back to a place that feels like home again.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

A Final Word

My dear,

You have now read twenty-one stories. Twenty-one women in twenty-one moments that marriage quietly asks of us. Their names were different. Their situations were specific. But you recognised something in each of them, even if only faintly, because the feelings they carried are not unique to them. They belong to all of us who have ever tried to love someone closely and honestly over a long time.

Marriage after the shaadi is not the romantic story. It is the real one. It is made of Tuesday evenings and unanswered texts and decisions made too quickly and apologies that arrive too late and small kindnesses that go unnoticed until they stop. It is also made of the moment you reach across the silence and choose each other again, not because it is easy, but because it matters.

Nothing in this book asked you to be perfect. It only asked you to be honest. Honest about what you feel. Honest about what you need. Honest about the gap between where you are and where you want to be. That honesty, held gently and without blame, is the beginning of everything that can get better.

You are allowed to want more from your marriage. You are allowed to be unhappy with what is not working while still loving the person beside you. You are allowed to grow, to change, to need things that shift over time. None of this makes you difficult. It makes you alive.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi
